title: Bounding the Maximum Length of Non-preemptive Regions under Fixed Priority Scheduling

extraction.paper_name: Bounding the Maximum Length of Non-Preemptive Regions Under Fixed Priority Scheduling
extraction.paper_description: This paper provides an exact method and two approximate methods for calculating the maximum length of non-preemptive regions (NP regions) that tasks can execute without violating the schedulability of a fixed-priority real-time system.

formal_description.statement: A task set T = {tau_1, tau_2, ..., tau_n} where each task tau_i is defined by (C_i, D_i, T_i) and indexed by decreasing priority.

variables.tau_i: The i-th task in the set
variables.C_i: Worst-case execution requirement of task i
variables.T_i: Period or minimum inter-arrival time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the basic task model for the system.

informal_sketch.intuition: Standard sporadic task model where tasks are ordered by priority.
steps: Represent each task as a tuple of execution time, deadline, and period
Sort tasks such that index i < j implies priority of tau_i > priority of tau_j
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Task:
    def __init__(self, C_i, D_i, T_i, priority_i):
        self.C_i = C_i
        self.D_i = D_i
        self.T_i = T_i
        self.priority = priority_i

# Tasks sorted by priority (tau_1 is highest)
task_set = sorted(tasks, key=lambda x: x.priority, reverse=True)
key_insights: Priority ordering is essential for the subsequent blocking and interference analysis.

variables.RBF_tau_i_t: Request Bound Function for task i over interval t

assumptions: Critical instant occurs at synchronous activation
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum workload requested by a single task tau_i in interval t.

informal_sketch.intuition: Calculates the maximum number of jobs task i can release in a window of size t, multiplied by its execution time.
steps: Divide interval t by period T_i
Take the ceiling to account for the job released at the start of the interval
Multiply by the worst-case execution time C_i
key_insights: This is the standard demand calculation for fixed-priority analysis.

variables.W_i_t: Cumulative execution request of task i and all higher priority tasks
variables.RBF_tau_j_t: Request bound function of task j

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total processor demand from tasks with priority greater than or equal to tau_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: Sum up the workload of the task itself and every task that has a higher priority.
steps: Iterate through all tasks from index 1 to i
Sum their individual RBF values for interval t
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_W_i_t(task_set, i, t):
    total_workload = 0
    for j in range(0, i): # Assuming 0-indexed for tau_1 to tau_i
        total_workload += compute_RBF(task_set[j], t)
    return total_workload
key_insights: W_i_t represents the total time the processor is busy with tau_i or higher priority tasks.

formal_description.statement: TS_tau_i = P_i_minus_1_D_i, where P_0_t = {t} and P_i_t = P_i_minus_1_floor_t_div_T_i_mul_T_i union P_i_minus_1_t
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the set of points in time that must be checked to verify schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: A reduced set of time points (discontinuities in the RBF) that are sufficient to check for the existence of a feasible schedule.
steps: Start with the deadline D_i
Recursively add points where higher priority tasks release new jobs
Filter points to stay within the range [C_i, D_i]
key_insights: Checking only these points significantly reduces the complexity of the schedulability test compared to checking all time increments.

variables.q_k: Length of the non-preemptive region of lower priority task k

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum delay tau_i can suffer due to a lower priority task executing non-preemptively.

informal_sketch.intuition: In fixed priority scheduling, a task can only be blocked by at most one non-preemptive region from any task with lower priority.
steps: Identify all tasks with priority lower than tau_i
Find the maximum length of their non-preemptive regions
key_insights: Only the largest NP region among all lower priority tasks matters.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum amount of blocking task i can tolerate without missing its deadline.

informal_sketch.intuition: The blocking tolerance is the maximum 'slack' available in the schedule for task i across all relevant testing points.
steps: For every point t in the testing set TS_tau_i
Calculate the difference between the time t and the workload W_i_t
The maximum of these differences is the tolerance
key_insights: This value represents the 'budget' available for lower priority tasks to execute non-preemptively.

formal_description.statement: A task set T with floating NP regions is schedulable if and only if for all tau_i in T, there exists t in TS_tau_i such that W_i_t + B_i <= t.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a necessary and sufficient condition for schedulability with NP regions.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task is schedulable if there is at least one point in time before its deadline where all its work and the blocking from lower priority tasks can be completed.
steps: For each task tau_i
Calculate blocking B_i
Check if any t in TS_tau_i satisfies the condition workload + blocking <= time
key_insights: This extends the standard Bini-Buttazzo test by adding the blocking factor B_i.

formal_description.statement: Q_1 = infinity; Q_i = min(Q_i_minus_1, beta_i_minus_1) for 2 <= i <= n.

variables.Q_i: Maximum length of NP region for task i
variables.beta_i_minus_1: Blocking tolerance of the task with priority immediately higher than i

assumptions: The original fully preemptive task set is schedulable
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a recursive formula to calculate the maximum NP region for each task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Task i's NP region can be as large as the minimum blocking tolerance of all tasks with higher priority than it.
steps: Set Q_1 to infinity (highest priority task cannot be blocked)
For each subsequent task i, the limit is the minimum of the previous task's limit and the previous task's tolerance
key_insights: The sequence of Q values is non-increasing. A lower priority task is constrained by the 'tightest' higher priority task.

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a lower-complexity (but suboptimal) estimate of blocking tolerance.

informal_sketch.intuition: Instead of checking all points in the testing set, just check the slack at the deadline.
steps: Calculate workload W_i at time D_i
Subtract from D_i
Ensure the result is non-negative
key_insights: Reduces complexity from pseudo-polynomial to O(i) for each task, but may underestimate the true tolerance.

formal_description.statement: beta_LL_i = max(0, T_i * U_lub_i - sum_{k=1 to i} U_k)

variables.beta_LL_i: Approximate blocking tolerance using Liu & Layland bound
variables.U_lub_i: Liu & Layland utilization bound for i tasks: i*(2^(1/i) - 1)

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a utilization-based estimate of blocking tolerance.

informal_sketch.intuition: Uses the conservative Liu & Layland utilization bound to determine how much extra 'blocking utilization' the system can handle.
steps: Calculate the L&L bound for i tasks
Subtract the sum of actual task utilizations
Multiply the remaining utilization by the period T_i to get a time value
key_insights: Extremely fast to compute but very pessimistic, especially as the number of tasks increases.
